claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-built FCC matrix is a supersaturated solid solution containing fine processing-induced secondary phases.
Elevated-temperature oxidizing exposure selectively oxidizes Ti and Cr at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Strongly reducing exposure can selectively deoxidize reactive elements and thereby initiate degradation.
Selective oxidation produces brittle secondary oxides or phases and adjacent compositional-depletion zones.
High-temperature exposure can cause an additional BCC phase to precipitate from an initially FCC HEA.
Ti and Cr depletion lowers the stacking-fault energy of the surrounding FCC matrix.
Lower stacking-fault energy facilitates transformation from FCC to a brittle BCC or intermetallic phase.
Oxidation-induced chemical and microstructural changes alter local dislocation and tensile-deformation behavior.
A reducing atmosphere preserves the metastable ductile microstructure because oxidation is absent or suppressed.
Oxidizing exposure will produce intergranular oxide layers and brittle secondary phases in this alloy.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce ductility and tensile or creep performance relative to the as-built baseline.
Reducing-atmosphere samples will show less or later degradation than oxidizing-atmosphere samples.
Oxide formation, brittle-phase transformation, and weakened interfacial cohesion create stress concentrations that can cause catastrophic failure under load.
The onset of catastrophic failure will correlate with an FCC-to-brittle-secondary-phase transition.
The as-built alloy has relatively high strength and ductility at elevated temperature.
The proposed degradation mechanism applies approximately from 700 to 1000 °C, where oxidation, reduction, and phase-evolution kinetics are active.
Systematically varying oxygen partial pressure at about 800 °C while holding exposure duration fixed can test whether gas chemistry governs the degradation.
Absence of atmosphere-dependent phase evolution and mechanical degradation, or absence of correlation between oxidation-induced changes and failure, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary allow strongly reducing conditions to drive deoxidation-related degradation, whereas the mechanism and predicted outcome state that reducing conditions preserve the ductile microstructure and limit or delay degradation.
